t: that they took possession of it from ownerless property or the property of a convert. That both performed an act of possession that grants ownership of a field without an owner, or of the field of a convert who has no heirs, and both acquired it (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 2:1).
the law of a divisible property. That it is suitable for division, as explained below, halakhah 4.

but if each of them knew his portion. For example, if at the time of acquisition each acquired a defined portion of the field, or when they inherited it from their father they agreed between themselves what each one's portion is.
to separate his portion from his fellow's portion. With a fence or partition.
he will not find with what to buy. He has no money to buy his fellow's portion.
whose father left them a bathhouse or an olive press. Which are not subject to the law of division.

if the father made them for rental, the rent is shared equally. If the father designated them for rental, they divide the rental money between them, and the rich one may not compel the poor one to change the designation of the place to personal use (Kesef Mishneh).
if the father made them for himself. That he used them himself.
he cannot compel his brother to rent them out. The poor one cannot compel the rich one to rent them to others.
and the rich one says to the poor one etc.. Although in practice the poor one has no way to use them, since he has no olives or slaves.
sell to me, and I will borrow and buy. He borrows money to buy the rich one's share.
or sells to others and buys. He sells the land and pays for the rich one's share from the money he is paid.
they rent it out. They rent it out.

for it is impossible for both to live together because of the damage of being seen etc.. For when a person uses the courtyard and his fellow sees him, this counts as damage (below 2:14). And since the courtyard is not large enough to be divided, a partition cannot be placed in the middle.
and likewise anything that is suitable for constant use. That a person needs daily.
a bedspread. A sheet or blanket.
according to the partners. According to the number of partners.

the smallest of them receives a portion that the name of the whole is called upon. That even the owner of the smallest share in the partnership will receive a portion still called by the name it had before it was divided.

but if the name of the whole is not called upon the portion. Either because its parts are different or because its form was lost when it became smaller and its name no longer applies to it (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Bava Batra 1:6).
how etc.. The measures mentioned here follow the Mishnah, and they vary from place to place according to local custom (Maggid Mishneh).

enough to sow nine kavs. A kav is a unit of volume equal to one sixth of a se'ah (about 1.38 liters). And enough to sow nine kavs is a measure of land in which such a quantity can be sown, that is, an area of 3750 square cubits (about 860 square meters).
enough to sow half a kav. An area of about 208 square cubits (about 50 square meters).
enough to sow three kavs. An area of 1250 square cubits (about 290 square meters).

in what case does this apply, in the Land of Israel and the like. And the measure in the Land of Israel is smaller because the soil there is harder to work (Meiri, Bava Batra 12a), and some explain that land there is more expensive (Rabbenu Gershom there), and some explain that the land of the Land of Israel is of higher quality (Tosafot there).
enough for a day's plowing. Enough for one laborer to work the whole day plowing the area.
the triclinium... the moran. Types of palaces.
they assess it in monetary terms. They estimate its value.
the excess. That which has enough for division.
for he says to him, "I do not wish to take a gift". For it is the way of the righteous and people of deeds not to accept gifts (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 12:17).

the courtyards of villages. In which each person builds his house freely and afterward they share the courtyard among themselves, and therefore each acquires four cubits in front of the entrance of his house. But in the courtyards of cities, where each one has a portion known in advance, the courtyard is divided without allotting four cubits to each entrance (R. Y. Migash, Bava Batra 11a, Maggid Mishneh).
four cubits in front of it, across the width of the whole entrance. For unloading the burden (below 5:3).
they do not divide it. For the possibilities where the law of division does not apply, see above 1:2.
as we have explained. Above 1:4.
even if it was ten cubits. Even if the width of the entrance is unusually large, it receives four cubits.
he designated a single entrance for himself. That only at this entrance does he unload his burden and bring in and take out.
an akhsadra. A roofed structure between the entrance of the house and the courtyard.

if he can enter it with his load. For example, there are no partitions at its front that obstruct the animal's entry, or it is usually free of objects (see the various explanations of the Rishonim on Bava Batra 11b).
an entrance hall. The entry room to the house.
a balcony. A raised place in the courtyard, reached from the courtyard by a flight of steps, from which the upper apartments are entered.
it has only four cubits. Corresponding to the width of the balcony's opening to the courtyard; four cubits are not reckoned for each and every house that opens onto the balcony.
a chicken coop. That opens onto the courtyard. [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah, the Rambam vocalizes the word differently.]
it does not have four cubits. Because the chickens can climb up into it or out of it, and the owner of the coop does not need four cubits to unload a burden (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 11b).

a house half of which is roofed and half not roofed... does not have four cubits. For a person usually puts his belongings in the half of the house that is not roofed. And even if the unroofed part is at the inner side of the house, he can pass through the roofed part and unload his burden on the unroofed side.
a sealed house. Whose entrance he blocked.
it has four cubits. Because the owner of the house may open the blockage.
he broke down its doorposts. He removed the doorposts and the lintel, thereby revealing that he no longer intends to use this entrance.
a house that does not have four cubits by four cubits. Such a house is not defined as a house for various purposes in halakhah (see, for example, Hilchot Rotzeach 11:1 and elsewhere).

and the manure of a courtyard is divided according to the entrances. The cost of removing manure from the courtyard is calculated by the number of entrances of each house (Maggid Mishneh in the name of R. Yosef Migash). Some explain that this refers to manure that the courtyard residents want to use to fertilize their fields, and the more entrances, the more manure is thrown from that house (Maggid Mishneh in the name of Rashi).

the king's billeting. The costs of hosting the soldiers whom the king sends to be quartered in the citizens' homes (Maggid Mishneh in the name of Rashi). Some explain that this refers to the manure left behind by the king's soldiers quartered in the courtyard (see Beit Yosef and Rema, Choshen Mishpat 172:9).
according to the number of people. According to the number of people in each house.
even though they ruin its name. For after the division, the name of the thing being divided will no longer be called on each part separately (as above 1:4).

in a single volume. Because cutting them while in one volume is a disgrace. Although a person may cut up holy writings he owns even when in one volume (Hilchot Sefer Torah 7:15), doing so for the sake of division is a disgrace (Rema, Choshen Mishpat 173:1).
but in two bindings. Separate volumes, which need not be cut.
for they acquired it from them when they wished. When they agreed to divide, they made a kinyan sudar about it (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
for this is a kinyan of words. An agreement to divide without clearly fixing the portions is not a substantive thing to which a kinyan can apply.
as we have explained. There, 5:14.
they cannot retract. Because at the time of the kinyan they clearly fixed what each one's portion is, the kinyan took effect.

and likewise if one went himself and took possession of his portion etc.. After each of them had determined his portion among themselves and did not make a kinyan, if one of them performed an act of possession on a particular portion, the other cannot retract.
brothers who divided. Their inheritance. The same applies to partners (Maggid Mishneh).

once the lot came up for one of them, all acquired. For example, they set the division to follow the order of their birth, with Simeon in the portion adjacent to the one that falls to Reuben, and Levi adjacent to Simeon, and so on. When the lot came up for Reuben, each of the brothers acquired his portion (Maggid Mishneh, and see further explanations there).

as purchasers from one another. As if they had bought from one another the portion each had in the jointly owned property. And since anyone who sells sells generously, when each sold his portion he left himself no right in the portion he sold (see Hilchot Mechirah 25:3).

and they have no right of way over one another. For access to their portion, for example if one took the inner house and the other the outer one, even though there had been a path between the portions beforehand.
and likewise he may block the window overlooking his portion. One may build on his portion even if the building rises opposite the other's windows and blocks them (Kesef Mishneh).
and he builds beside the ladder even though he nullifies its use. He builds on his portion opposite the ladder, even though by building he prevents the other from climbing the ladder.
from the damages in which the sellers had established a right. The buyers acquired from them that same right to cause damage.
so that his friend will not see him when he uses his portion. That his friend not see him while he uses his courtyard.
and he has no presumptive right in the courtyard. One cannot prevent the other on the claim that the courtyard's condition without a partition was already established.
he may compel him to make a partition whenever he wishes. Because a person does not waive a permanent harm of this kind (see below 11:4).

and how wide should it be? Everything follows the custom of the locality. The thickness of the wall varies according to the material of which it is made (as below halakhah 18), and this is determined by the wall that the people of the locality customarily build when partners divide such a property between them.
and with branches. Branches.
how high is the wall. In a courtyard.

with a partition ten handbreadths high. For there is no harm of sight in a garden, since it is not intended for a person's use, and a partition is made there only to protect against theft (see Responsa of the Rambam, no. 395).
in a valley. A grain field.
he withdraws into his own and builds. He builds the wall on his own portion.

a marker of about a cubit with plaster on the outside. A marker made by plastering the wall to the extent of a cubit on his friend's side. He does not plaster on his own side, because the other could also plaster on his side and claim that the wall is his or both of theirs. And there is no concern that his friend will scrape off the plaster, because the place of scraping is noticeable (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 1:2, based on Babylonian Talmud ibid. 4b).

even in a place where it is customary not to fence gardens. In the case of a sale, they compel even in a place where it is not customary to fence, because the seller's intent is that the buyer remove all the damages that could be caused to the seller or to the fields adjacent to him (Maggid Mishneh, and see Hilchot Mechirah 21:22).
which are not hewn. Not dressed, and therefore wide.
of hewn stone. Dressed stones.
with half-bricks. Bricks cut in half, where one lays half a brick here and half a brick there with mortar between them (so a wall built of them is thicker than one of whole bricks).
up to a height of four cubits. With this the harm of sight is removed (above 2:16).
beyond four we do not obligate him. Even if it was higher before it fell.

we obligate him to give his share for the height opposite his wall. For by building a wall higher than four cubits opposite the shared wall, he reveals that he wishes to use the raised height of the shared wall.
to make a house for himself. For he intends to place a roof on the two walls.

he is presumed to have paid. For since this law of sharing the wall's costs is known to all, certainly one partner would not have built the whole wall at his own expense without claiming from his neighbor (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 1:4).
and he swears a heset oath that he paid. A heset oath is a rabbinic oath for one who is sued and denies everything (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3).
he is not believed. For this law and its details are not known, and presumably he did not pay for the wall above four cubits (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
he swears while holding a sacred object. While holding a Torah scroll in his hand (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
like all who swear and collect. For the Sages enacted that they may swear and collect (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:2).

a ruin among the ruins of his friend. His friend's ruins surround his ruin on all sides. And in a ruin, as in a valley, there is no obligation to fence to remove the harm of sight except where it is the custom (as above 2:16).
and his friend arose and fenced. Built a fence between himself and his friend.
from the expense. From the cost of the fence that his friend built.
and his ruin is open to the public domain as it was. On the side left without a fence.
they roll over. They obligate.
up to four cubits. Up to a height of four cubits, even if the fence was higher (as above halakhah 1).
for only a small amount is rolled over onto him. The one who is enclosed is not obligated to pay half the cost, but must give money as the judges see fit.
he revealed his mind. That he benefits from the fence.
and their roofs were made for dwelling. That they are used for daily use.
even if they were on the two sides of the public domain. Although people in the public domain can also see the roof's users when they use it.
a parapet. Four cubits high.

this not opposite that, and extends beyond. Each makes a parapet on a different side of his roof and extends its length slightly to make sure they cannot see each other by looking from the side of the parapet.
and you always see me. Even at night, and even when I am sitting.
a roof adjacent to the courtyard of his friend. And both are at the same height.

he makes for himself a parapet four cubits high. The owner of the roof must make a parapet so as not to harm the courtyard's owner by sight (but the courtyard's owner does not harm the roof's owner, because the roof is not made for dwelling, and even if it is made for dwelling, its use is not as frequent as the use of a courtyard - see Maggid Mishneh and Sema 160:2).
between one roof and another of the other roofs. That are not made for dwelling.
so that he catch him as a thief if he enters his property. To define the extent of his property, so that if another enters without permission, he is considered as having entered to steal.
two courtyards, one above the other. And the upper one harms the lower by its sight.

the upper one may not say 'I will build opposite me and go up,' but both build from below. When the upper owner cannot build a wall from his ground upward (for example, the ground is not strong enough) and it must be built from the lower owner's ground, the upper owner cannot evade sharing the cost of the part of the wall up to the start of his courtyard, because this part is needed for the continuation of the wall that removes the harm of sight. And the lower owner shares in this part of the wall, though he does not harm the upper one by sight, because he benefits from being able to use it, and because the wall prevents stones and earth from crumbling from the side of the upper courtyard (Ramah, Bava Batra 6b).

the upper owner need not do anything for the lower owner. The owner of the upper courtyard has no obligation toward the owner of the roof because he does not harm him, since the roof is not set for use.
they do not listen to him. For he cannot compel his friend to take the stones.
hin. Yes.
and he cannot retract. The owner of the wall.
and even if he said to him. The owner of the wall to the owner of the garden after he had cleared the stones.
your expenses. The costs of removing the stones.

for he said it only to put him off. The reason he told him 'they are yours' is not that he intends to transfer ownership to him, but to put off the garden's owner so that he not press him to clear the stones from his garden.
five gardens supplied with water from one spring etc.. They receive water from the spring, and the spring flows from garden to garden, and the water channel broke.
all of them repair with the uppermost. The owners of the lower gardens share in the repair costs of those above them, because their gardens need the flow of water that reaches them from there.
five courtyards that pour water into one drain. They drain waste water through one sewer pipe that passes from the upper courtyard to the lower ones.
with the lowest. Because all of them need the water to flow out through the lowest.
the people of the river. Whose fields are by the river, and the river flows by itself into the channels and waters the fields.
they water in order. The upper ones first and the lower ones afterward.
if one of them wished to dam it so that the water would return to him and he could water first. To stop the water's flow near his channels so that the water enters his field.
whoever overpowers, wins. We do not interfere in this matter; the people will sort it out among themselves.
and a cistern. Which they dig near the water channel so that when the channel dries up, they can draw water from the cistern.

the nearest fills first for the sake of the ways of peace. Because people are more particular about the cistern, since they fear the channel may dry up, the Sages enacted that the nearest one fills first for the sake of the ways of peace (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 170:2).
an upper story. A second floor.
the owner of the upper story gives him nothing toward his expenses. The owner of the upper story need not participate with the owner of the house in building the wall that fell.
and he compels the owner of the house to build it as it was. Because the upper story rests on the house.
and the ceiling. The beams of which the ceiling is built.
it belongs to the owner of the house. If it weakened beneath him, he must repair it.
and the plaster layer above the ceiling. The covering of mortar over the beams.

it belongs to the owner of the upper story. Because the purpose of the plaster layer is to level the floor of the upper owner for his benefit. This law applies specifically to two partners; but if the owner of the house rented out the upper story, the owner of the house must repair the plaster layer as well (Hilchot Sechirut 6:4).
both of them. The owner of the house and the owner of the upper story.
if the upper fell on the lower and destroyed it. In this case the broken stones belong to the upper story.
or the lower slipped away and the upper fell and was destroyed. In this case the broken stones belong to the house.
to build the house. At his own expense, after the house and the upper story have fallen.
that he must give him. The owner of the house.
neither of them is able to build. For example, both are poor.

if they were stones and he wishes to change them to bricks. For example, they were undressed stones six handbreadths thick, or dressed stones five handbreadths thick, and he now wants to build with bricks three handbreadths thick.
he increased the windows or added to the height of the house. Since this weakens the walls.
the beams of the house sagged and descended into the airspace of the house. The beams of the house's ceiling loosened and the ceiling sank down into the interior of the house.

if they reached within ten handbreadths, he demolishes and builds. When the house no longer has the ten-handbreadth height that is the minimum for dwelling, the house is not liable to the upper story, and the owner of the house demolishes and rebuilds the ceiling, and the upper owner the plaster layer (as above halakhah 1).
the owner of the upper story can hold him back. From demolishing the building for the renovation, claiming he does not want to leave the upper story for the duration of the renovation.

they stipulated between themselves about this matter. That if the beams descend into the airspace of the house, the owner of the house may demolish and repair, and they did not fix the height between them.
an average bundle. Of reeds, at which height people usually live.
in the thickness of the mountain. In a cave hewn in the rock of a mountain.
and the garden of another. A garden belonging to another person.
and the ceiling of the olive press sagged by four handbreadths or more. The ceiling of the olive press weakened and sank over an area of four handbreadths or more.

the owner of the garden goes down and sows below. Since it is troublesome to work a garden on two levels, the owner of the olive press must allow the garden's owner to sow in the area of the olive press as the area of his whole garden (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 117b).
arches. A structure of arches to strengthen the ceiling.
and the upper one repairs the ground of his garden. He brings earth to the garden.
two gardens one on top of the other. Adjacent to one another, one low and one high, and vegetables grow in the height of the earth between them.
from its root. From its roots.
so that he not endanger himself. That he not stretch too far and put himself at risk of falling (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 10:8).
to its foliage. The stalks of the vegetable.
they do not take it from his hand. As with any monetary doubt, one does not take from the one in possession.
on the boundary. On the border between two fields.
that it leans. That its foliage leans.
a river swept away his olive trees and planted them in his friend's field. The river uprooted olive trees from his field and carried them to his friend's field, where they were naturally planted.
and the other said, 'I will take my olive trees'. The owner of the trees wishes to take his trees back.
for the sake of the settlement of the land. For uprooting planted trees harms the settlement of the land.
with their clumps of soil. The clumps of earth around the tree, by whose power the tree can live even if uprooted from the ground (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 10:12).

the owner of the field and the owner of the olives divide the fruit for three years. When the olive trees were uprooted with their clumps, there is no need to wait anew for the three years of orlah before eating from them. So during these years the owner of the field benefits from the owner of the olives' clumps of earth and therefore shares with him (see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 101a).

and if they were not uprooted with their clumps, everything goes to the owner of the land immediately. And although the fruit is orlah and he may not eat it, he nevertheless acquires the trees themselves (Maggid Mishneh).
one who sells his olive trees for wood. He sold the trees so that the buyer would cut them down, keeping the land for himself, and before the buyer cut them down the olive trees produced fruit.

if he stipulated with him to cut immediately, all the fruit they produce belongs to the owner of the land. Because they grew from his land, and the buyer cannot acquire it on account of his trees growing it, since he was required to cut them immediately.

and if he stipulated with him that he cut whenever he wishes, all the fruit they produce belongs to the owner of the trees. For he left him the olive trees as they are, and the profit they yield belongs to the buyer.
unspecified. Without stipulating.

less than a revi'it per se'ah. The olives are poor and a se'ah of olives yields less than a quarter-log of oil (a ratio of less than one to ninety-six; Rashi, Bava Metzia 100b, and see other explanations of the Rishonim there).
apart from the expense. The measure of a revi'it is after deducting the costs of picking and pressing the olives.
belongs to the owner of the olive trees. The buyer, since the owner of the land waives such poor olives.

they divide. For from a revi'it and above people are particular and do not give up, and since they are partners in the olives - for they grew from the seller's land and the buyer's trees - they divide the profit.
a courtyard of partners. Onto which several houses open.
an entrance hall. A small structure built at the courtyard gate.
carving and painting. Sculpting and engraving on walls to decorate them.
one of them did it on his own. One of the partners did one of the things for which they do not compel.
they roll over everything onto him. They obligate him to share his part of the expenses of his friend (see a similar law above 3:1).
one who has a house in another courtyard. And does not live there.
a door, a bolt and a lock. For these are made to guard the courtyard.
and a bolt. A bar.
in other matters. That are not made to guard the courtyard, such as an entrance hall.

since it is not the way of the daughters of Israel to be shamed at the riverbank. There is immodesty in doing laundry there, and therefore the partners must allow the women to do laundry inside the courtyard and cannot prevent it.
an alley that is not a through-way. A small street open to the public domain on one side.

he may hold him back whenever he wishes. For partners do not necessarily mind occasional uses of the courtyard, and therefore the fact that he did not protest does not express consent and waiver of this use as a permanent matter.
established a right. He established a right to use, and it cannot be prevented from him.
because partners are particular about the partition. For this is a permanent matter, and the lack of protest indicates consent and waiver.
by way of a loan. That the courtyard's owner lends him the use of his courtyard, and when he wishes he will remove him.
there is no person who lends space to his friend. Out of concern that the borrower might claim that he established a right to do so.
to the courtyard. That is shared by him and his friend.

his friend can hold him back because he looks at him from it. Even if there is another window through which he can look, he may prevent him from opening an additional window, because a person has no right to add to the existing harm of sight (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 3:9).
and if he opened it, he must block it. And if he did not protest, or they helped him build the window, see below 7:6.

and likewise partners may not open in their courtyard a house entrance opposite a house entrance etc.. Even if they gave each other permission, so that every person will have a measure of privacy and modesty.
to the public domain, entrance opposite entrance etc.. With the public domain between them.
for the people of the public domain pass by and go. And do not linger opposite the entrance.
who bought a house in another courtyard. Adjacent to the first courtyard.
he cannot open his entrance. From the new house.
even if he built an upper story over his house. And the upper story opens to his house and not to the courtyard.
because he increases the traffic on them. Since additional people pass through and use the courtyard.
he opens the entrance of the upper story into his house. Since they must pass through his house, he will not bring many people there.

and if he wished to divide his room into two, he may divide. For he is not adding another entrance to the courtyard, and one who enters the second room passes through the first room, and there is no concern that he will increase the number of residents in the courtyard because of this.
an entrance of one of the partners. Facing the courtyard.
with two I cannot. For I do not know which of them you use each time.

his friend opposite him cannot hold him back. The owner of the house on the other side of the public domain does not stop him, for the other could argue against him that he is no different from the people of the public domain who can see him (as above halakhah 6).

to make for them a side-post and a beam for the alley. A vertical post at the side of the entrance, or a beam placed horizontally above it, by making which it is permitted to carry in the alley on the Sabbath (see Hilchot Shabbat 17:2).

the residents of the alley cannot compel him to make a door for the alley. They cannot compel him to share in the cost of building a door at the alley's entrance. He can even hold them back and prevent them from building this door (Maggid Mishneh).
that I enter with my bundle up to my entrance. The lintel of the door and the need to open it might keep him from entering easily with his load.
and the residents of the alley wished to set up doors for themselves. At the two entrances of the alley.
and they enter it. They need to enter the alley because of crowding in the public domain.

one who wished to open an entrance in an alley that is not a through-way. He wants to open an entrance from his courtyard to an alley he is not accustomed to (Rashi, Bava Batra 11b). Some explain that his courtyard lies between two alleys and opens to one alley, and now he wishes to open an entrance on the side of the other alley as well, and thereby the residents of the second alley would be able to enter their alley through his entrance (Rosh, ibid. 1:40).
he may open any entrance he wishes at the outset. Because people of the public domain also sometimes pass through it.
he broke down its doorposts. He removed the doorposts and the lintel, thereby revealing that he no longer intends to use this entrance (see also above 2:7).
and to move it to another alley. His courtyard lies between two alleys, and he wishes to block the entrance he had to one alley and open one in its place to the other alley.
the residents of the alley can hold him back. From blocking the entrance.
a tax will come upon them. A general tax will be imposed on them.
they use it together with the outer one. The area opposite the entrance of the courtyard adjacent to the alley's entrance.
and the outer one uses for itself. But it does not use together with the inner ones the area opposite their entrances.
a platform. A raised structure on which objects are placed or on which people sit.
the outer one cannot hold him back. For the owner of the outer courtyard may not use this area.
who opened a second entrance to his courtyard. Facing the alley.

the outer one cannot hold him back, since it may use only from its entrance outward. And the inner ones do not hold him back either, because the right of use in this area is shared by all the inner courtyards (see Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh).

but if he opened the second entrance between himself and the third, the inner ones can hold him back. Because in this area the owner of the second courtyard has no right of use, only the owners of the courtyards from the third inward.
a wall, doors and a bar for the city. To protect the city.
and to build for them a synagogue etc.. See also Hilchot Tefillah 11:1.
for the sake of the settlement of the Land of Israel. For by means of the roads additional people will arrive and settle in it.
the people of a valley. An open area containing fields of several people.
a trench and the son of a trench. Channels six and three handbreadths wide to protect the fields (see Hilchot Mechirah 21:22).
one who has a courtyard in another city. And does not live there.
cisterns, pits and caves. Used for storing water.
whoever is adjacent to the wall gives more. Since the danger from an enemy outside is greater the nearer one is to the wall.
and anyone who lives in the city twelve months. Who lives in the city as a renter.
or who bought a dwelling house in it. In which case, immediately upon buying the house he becomes like the other residents of the city.
except for Torah scholars etc.. And they are also exempt from paying taxes, whether a fixed tax on the city's residents or a tax fixed per individual (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:10).
they return to them everything that was taken from them. Because orphans do not waive money (see, for example, Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 15:16).
not to settle among them a tailor or a tanner. Because their work might disturb the residents of the alley.
tanner. One who processes hides.
a miller. A grinder with millstones.
he cuts off my livelihood. He ruins my livelihood.
a convert from another country. A native of another city.
the king's portion. Taxes.
he cannot prevent him. Even the first craftsman cannot prevent him on the claim that he ruins his livelihood.
the residents of the alley compel. That is not a through-way.
peddlers. Who sell spices.
those who travel around. Who go about.
the people of the towns cannot hold them back. On the claim that these peddlers reduce their livelihood.
for it is an enactment of Ezra. Ezra the Scribe made ten enactments, and this is one of them (see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 82a).
so that perfumes will be available to the daughters of Israel. And they will not become repulsive to their husbands.
and if he is a Torah scholar. The peddler is also a Torah scholar.
he sets up wherever he wishes. So that he is not disturbed from his studies.
the people of the city can hold them back. Because by this they harm the local merchants.
on market day. On the day when a fair is held.
and if they have a loan in the city. And they wish to remain in the city and earn from their merchandise until they repay the loan.
an alley that is not a through-way. But an alley that is a through-way to the public domain has the law of the public domain (see above 5:14).
a craftsman. A bloodletter.
a weaver. One who weaves.
and not to a Jewish scribe who writes the documents. A scribe who writes various documents.
and not a teacher of gentile children. For there is no commandment in this.
the neighbors can protest against him. Even if he established a right to do his work in the courtyard, they can at any time protest his bringing his customers there (as below 11:5).
for he established a right to do so. And they did not protest, but at the outset they can prevent him (as above halakhah 8).
he may teach Jewish children Torah inside his house. But if he teaches them arithmetic or geometry and the like, they can hold him back (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 2:3).

one who has a cistern inside his friend's house. For example, he bought the cistern from him and was given a way to reach it, or in the case of partners or brothers who divided and agreed among themselves that the cistern's owner would have a path to reach his cistern, and this path passes through his friend's courtyard.

he enters at the time when people usually enter etc.. But he may not enter and leave at hours when people do not usually enter and leave their homes, and thereby trouble the owner of the house to get up and open for him.

and he may not bring in his animal and water it from his cistern. For the transfer or agreement about passage in his friend's courtyard is not a full transfer but a right of way, and it does not include these uses.
and both of them make a cover over the cistern. Each of them makes a lock to lock the cistern.

so that no one enters there except with his knowledge. So that the house owner's wife does not enter the cistern's enclosure without her husband's knowledge and become secluded with the cistern's owner (see Torat Chaim, Bava Batra 99b).

one who has a garden inside his friend's garden. He bought the inner garden and was given a path to his garden; also heirs or partners who divided, and the outer owner agreed to give the inner owner passage through his garden. Since the path is not entirely acquired by him but only the right to pass through it, he may use the path only for things necessary for the garden and not for anything else.
merchants. Traders who come to buy vegetables from his garden.

and the outer one may sow the path. If he wishes. For the path is acquired by the inner one only for passage, and he cannot prevent the outer one from anything so long as he does not prevent his passage to his garden.
they moved the path to the side. They agreed among themselves that passage to the inner garden would be along the side and not through the middle of the outer garden.

he enters at the time he wishes etc.. Since it is a side path, the owner of the outer garden loses nothing by it, and presumably gave the inner garden's owner the option to walk this path without restriction and to bring merchants through it.

and he may not enter through it into another field. For if he does so, he increases the walking on the owner of the second garden, and the path was given to him only for the garden, even when it is at the side (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 6:6).
and each of them can hold back the other from sowing the path they set at the side. Since they agreed that the path would be at the side, they designated it for walking and not for sowing.
for he has established a right to this harm. For the window existed before the courtyard and he is in possession of it.
and if his friend came to build a wall opposite the window to remove the harm of his sight. So that the owner of the window not look at him.
so that he does not darken it for him. So that he does not block the light from the owner of the window.
to build opposite it at a distance of four cubits. So as not to block the light.

and to raise the building four cubits etc.. That the wall be four cubits or more above the top of the window, so that the courtyard's owner cannot look through his friend's window and harm him by sight.
and he does not harm him by sight. Because of the difference in height between the top of the wall and the start of the window's height.
he built one wall beside the window. The wall stands perpendicular to his friend's window.
he must distance it from the window a handbreadth. So as not to darken the window.
and raise the wall four cubits above the window. He builds the wall four cubits or more above the top of the window.
he bends the top of the wall. He makes the edge of the wall pointed.
there must be a width of four cubits between them. A handbreadth's distance on each side is not enough, because building two walls darkens the window considerably even though they are at its sides.

and the window in the middle of the four. Not necessarily exactly in the middle, but there must be four cubits between the two walls, and in any case neither may be less than a handbreadth from the window (see Maggid Mishneh).

therefore etc.. Just as one who builds a wall must distance it four cubits from the height of his friend's window, lest he peer in and see into his house, so one who wishes to open a window to his friend's courtyard can be held back by his friend, on the claim that he could harm him by sight (Lechem Mishneh).
that it is high. Above the floor of the house.
and the courtyard's owner waived it for him. Explicitly.
and helped him. In opening the window.

a courtyard owner cannot build opposite it or at its sides unless he distances four cubits. Because the right arising from the courtyard owner's waiver in such windows includes the courtyard owner's responsibility not to harm the window's owner by sight or darkening.
as we have explained. Above, halakhot 1-5.
when he opened it for use. For example, to place objects in the window space.
and his friend came to build in front of them. And thereby darken his friend's windows or harm him by sight.
that I should go to the trouble from place to place. In moving his residence to another place.

the trait of Sodom. A reprehensible trait resembling the conduct of the people of Sodom. Its essence is that a person refuses to let others benefit from what is his even when no harm or loss comes to him from it.
I will open another small one. In another place.

two brothers who divided etc.. Brothers who divided a courtyard they inherited from their father, and in this division they valued the price of the wood and bricks and not the use of the courtyard's airspace.
the courtyard is laid out as a garden. A courtyard made for decoration.
the akhsadra. A roofed structure between the entrance of the house and the courtyard.

one who wishes to put out a projection from his wall etc.. When his wall is adjacent to his friend's courtyard, and the owner of the wall wishes to extend a protruding structure from his wall into the airspace of his friend's courtyard.
and the courtyard's owner did not protest immediately. Enough time passed that presumably the courtyard's owner noticed the projection and was silent (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 3:8).
to build beneath the projection and nullify its use. To build a structure beneath the projection in such a way that it would not be possible to hang things on it and use it.
and extended in the air. Extending in length into the courtyard's airspace.

he established a right to four by four. Since the measure of a significant place is four handbreadths by four handbreadths, when he agreed to the length of a significant place, he also agreed to the width of a significant place (Rashbam, Bava Batra 59b).
the owner of the border. His neighbor, the owner of the courtyard (in some versions: 'the owner of the courtyard').
rungs. Steps.

he did not establish a right to this harm. Because this ladder is small and is moved from place to place, a person is not particular about its being placed on his property, and this does not constitute a right (see above 5:5).

and if it was a large ladder with four rungs or more, he established a right. Because of its size it is not moved and presumably stands fixed there, and since he did not protest, the ladder's owner established a right.

but if he placed a small one, he cannot prevent him. If at the moment the ladder is not a nuisance, the courtyard's owner cannot prevent the ladder's owner from placing it on the claim that he does not want him to establish a right, for a small ladder carries no right (and because he loses nothing by it, he may not hold him back, as above 7:8 - Maggid Mishneh).
one who wishes to put a pipe out over his friend's courtyard so that water will flow there. For example, he wishes to keep waste water away from his wall and the like.
a gutter. A long spout attached to the wall that channels rainwater from the roof into his friend's courtyard.
the courtyard's owner can hold him back. Since he wants to use this water to water his animal or garden and the like.
and move it to another side. To transfer it to another place in the courtyard.
for a pipe is not made for use like a projection, so that it would establish a right in the courtyard's airspace. As above, halakhah 2.
the water drips. From many places along the roof.
like a tent. A sloped structure from which all the water runs down and drips in a strong stream.
this one digs from this side. He makes a recess in the wall in order to rest the beam in it.
and he inserts his beams, whatever they are. Small or large.

even if it was small and Simeon wished to replace it with a large, thick beam, he may replace. For presumably Reuben's waiver is not only regarding the thin beam, but a beam suited to the weight of the wall, even if thicker (Meiri, Bava Batra 6a).
I waived and let you place it only because it is temporary. He thought that he had permitted the beam only for the time being and that it would soon be removed, and therefore did not protest.
a festival sukkah. For the festival of Sukkot.

after seven days he has established a right. Although for an ordinary sukkah thirty days are needed, since this is a sukkah for a mitzvah and Simeon did not take it down immediately after the festival, he proves that he intends to leave it there permanently, and therefore if Reuben did not protest, he established a right (Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Batra 6b in the name of Rabbenu Yonah).
for he waived only for one. The wall's owner waived only for the insertion of one beam.
that he swear a heset oath. An oath the Sages enacted for one who is sued and denies everything (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3).
for he has no use of it. For Simeon's beams are not resting there now.
it will collapse. It will fall down.
a cistern... a trench... a cave. Various forms of water reservoirs.

they distance... three handbreadths or plaster with lime. These things weaken the wall when they touch it (because they heat up on their own or for other reasons), and therefore one must separate them from the wall by distancing them from it or by means of lime.
the pressed olive residue. The olive waste after the oil has been extracted.
the manure. Organic waste useful for fertilizing the soil, such as animal droppings or fruit peels.
the rocks. Which tend to crumble and thereby spoil the soil and loosen it (Tosafot, Bava Batra 19a in the name of Rabbenu Chananel).
they distance the seeds. Because they weaken the ground and bring up soft earth, and through this the wall's foundation is loosened and damaged.
and the plow. Plowing the ground, even if he does not sow there, since plowing loosens the ground and spoils the wall's foundation.
they distance the millstones. From the wall.

three handbreadths from the lower millstone, which is four from the upper. The mill is made of two stones, and the lower stone is a handbreadth wider than the upper (see the diagram on the next page).
so that it not move it. For the movement of the millstones can shake the wall.
or so that the sound of the millstones not startle him. For the noise of the millstones can make the wall vibrate and damage it.
three from its base, which is four from its rim. Because the base of the oven is wider than its rim.
against a brick wall. For when water is poured on bricks they dissolve.
bare rock. Exposed rock.
from the dovecote. His friend's dovecote.

the gutter. A long spout attached to the wall that channels rainwater from the roof to his friend's courtyard, and sometimes it breaks or becomes clogged and must be cleaned of dirt and other things that obstruct the flow of water.

since he established a right in it. Since he established a right for water to be poured from the gutter into his friend's courtyard (see above 8:5), he also established a right to repair the gutter from within his friend's courtyard (Maggid Mishneh).
like a gamma. A right angle, similar to the Greek letter gamma, whose form is Γ. That is, he built a wall perpendicular to his friend's wall.
opposite Simeon's wall. Parallel to his wall.
so that many people trample it and the ground is strengthened. For people's treading between the walls firms and hardens the ground, which benefits the wall.
in a garden wall. Where people do not walk much because of the seeds.
or in the wall of a courtyard in a new city. Where the ground adjacent to the wall has not been trodden enough and strengthened.
adjacent to his friend's boundary. Adjacent to the border of his friend's field, where there is no wall or cistern.
it is not made for cisterns. For example, a field that is satisfied with rainwater alone and does not need irrigation from cisterns.
and if his friend decides. To dig a cistern in it although it is not suited for that.
until there is a thickness of six handbreadths between the cavities of the two cisterns. So that the wall of each cistern is three handbreadths thick.
the house and the upper story belong to two people. The house to one and the upper story to another.
the owner of the house shall not make an oven in his house. He shall not set up a clay baking oven, which gives off great heat, lest the ceiling above it be burned.
unless he has over it. From the top of the oven's height to the ceiling above it.
until there is a plaster layer beneath it three handbreadths. A covering of mortar over the floor, so that the ceiling beneath it is not burned.
and for a stove. Whose heat is less than that of an oven.
a baker's oven. Of bakers, which is heated all day and is very hot.

as explained in its place. Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 14:2, that if a person lit a fire on his property and the fire spread and caused damage, he is liable to pay (and although it was explained there that one who distances fire from his friend's field by the proper measure is exempt, the Rishonim distinguished between the cases and wrote that in the distancing discussed here, since these are things in a person's constant use, the Sages could not require a large distance, and therefore a person has an obligation at all times to guard himself from causing damage, and if he did not, he is liable - Rif, Bava Kamma 25b, Shakh, Choshen Mishpat 155:2, Netivot HaMishpat ibid. 1).
a storehouse. A warehouse.
alfalfa. Alfalfa, grain fodder.
a baker. A bakery.
a dyer. A place where cloth is dyed.

a wine storehouse in the Land of Israel. For the wine of the Land of Israel is stronger than the wine of other lands, and the heat and smoke rising from the house beneath it improve it (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 20b).
he cannot protest against him. He cannot protest against the owner of the house that he not make a stable and the like in it, because he already established a right to this.

the owner of the upper story swept and sprinkled his upper story or added windows. He cleaned, aired and prepared the upper story for use as a storehouse, and thereby revealed his intention to make a storehouse.

sesame, pomegranates, dates and the like. With regard to these fruits there is a doubt whether fire and stench harm them (R. Yosef Migash, Bava Batra 20b). Some explained that fire and stench do not harm these fruits, but by bringing them into the upper story the storehouse owner revealed that he intends to make a storehouse there even for things that are spoiled by heat and stench (Rabbenu Gershom, ibid.).
a partition. He built an upper story inside his shop that separates his shop from the storehouse, and possibly no damage will come from it to the upper story.

in all of these the owner of the storehouse can hold him back. Although in these cases we are in doubt whose right prevails, the shop owner has no permission to harm his friend on the basis of doubt (Maggid Mishneh).
the owner of the storehouse cannot remove the oven in any of these. As with any monetary doubt, if one came first and acquired, his friend cannot hold him back until he brings proof.
and the carob and the sycamore. Whose branches are many and spread a great distance.
for the beauty of the city. For it is a beauty to a city to have open space in front of it. [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah the Rambam writes and vocalizes the word for 'beauty' differently.]

and if the tree came first, the people of the city give him its value. One of the townspeople cuts it down and afterward collects its value from the townspeople and pays the tree's owner (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 2:7).

the tree's owner has no payment. For the tree must be cut in any case, whether the tree came first or the city did; and since it is being cut, as to the payment we say to him, 'Bring proof that the tree came first and take payment' (ibid.).

a permanent threshing floor. A threshing floor where winnowing is done with the special winnowing tool, and since he throws the grain upward the chaff flies far (Maggid Mishneh, Kesef Mishneh, based on Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 24b). Some explain that this refers to a floor where winnowing is done regularly, but for occasional winnowing no distancing is needed (Sema).
so that the chaff not harm his friend's plantings. For the chaff penetrates the plantings and dries and spoils them.
his fallow field. A plowed field before it is sown.
the tannery. A place for processing hides.
a flax soaking pit. Water in which flax is soaked.
leeks. Leeks.
for they weaken its taste. They reduce the sharpness of the onion.
for the bees eat the leaves and spoil the honey. For eating mustard gives sharpness and bitterness to the honey and spoils it.
and the damage comes to his friend by itself. And not from the hand of the one who placed it.
and likewise all the distancing mentioned above regarding this matter. In this chapter and the previous one.
it is as if he damaged with his arrows. Like a person who throws an arrow and causes damage by it; this act is attributed to the person and he is called a damager.
the owner of an upper story who was pouring water. On the floor of the upper story.
a plaster layer in which the water is absorbed when poured. A layer of mortar that absorbs the water.
within sixteen cubits are Simeon's roots. Up to this distance the roots draw from Simeon's ground.
so that it not obstruct the plow. For the plow reaches a depth of three handbreadths.
he must distance four cubits. For the sake of working the field, so that when he plows his trees he will not need to bring his plow into his friend's field.
in the Land of Israel. For its soil is rich and the roots spread farther (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 2:12).
his friend's tree leans. The tree's branches spread into his friend's field.

the full height of an ox-goad on top of the plow. He cuts the branches up to the height of the goad stick with which the cattle are driven during plowing, when it stands on top of the plow, so that the trees' branches do not obstruct him in plowing (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 2:13).
and the carob and the sycamore. Which have much shade that harms the field.
he cuts all that leans until it is balanced opposite the boundary. He cuts all the branches that lean beyond the border between the fields.
an irrigated field. A field that needs watering.
he cuts all that leans. For the trees' shade harms the irrigated field and the trees, because it keeps the dew from them (ibid.).
one who made a threshing floor. A non-permanent threshing floor; but a permanent threshing floor must be distanced fifty cubits (as above 10:2, Lechem Mishneh).
and even by the usual wind. Although he does not cause the damage with his hands, if the damage results from the usual wind, he must distance.
for all of these are as if he damaged with his arrows. As above 10:5.
ground wheat. Wheat kernels that are split into several parts by pounding.
until the lid of the barrel shakes on the mouth of the barrel. If one places a barrel in the courtyard, the barrel's lid will be shaken.
for the damage comes from his force. For the damage comes directly from his pounding and not through the help of something else (such as wind and the like, mentioned in the previous halakhah).
as we have explained. Above 6:12, 7:1, 7:6, 8:1 and elsewhere.

and likewise the harm of sight in a place that requires a partition. For example, in a courtyard of partners and the like. But one who opens a window or projection toward his friend's courtyard, even though he can harm him from there by sight, has a right (as above 7:6, 8:1, and see Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 154:8 who gave the reason for this).
as we have explained. Above 2:14.
they changed. They were altered.
and if they made a kinyan from his hand. That they made a kinyan sudar on the waiver (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
the work of blood. A bloodletter.

if his friend was particular. Although people in general are not particular about these things, if this person is known as someone whose mind cannot bear these things and is established as such, he may protest (Maggid Mishneh).
an alley. That is not a through-way (see above 6:11).

and they did not protest against him, for he established a right. For at the outset they could have held him back from doing so there, but if they did not protest he established a right, even if his work is noisy (see halakhah 12 there).
and they were silent. His neighbors.
he did not establish a right in this matter. Although he established a right to do his work in the house, they can protest against him that he not sell there.
and on this the Geonim ruled. In this manner.
who opened a window. Above 7:6.
diverted the water channel. Above 9:1.
you waived for me. Explicitly.

the injured party must bring proof. Since the right in these damages is acquired immediately, the damager is in possession, and the injured party who challenges the right must bring proof (Maggid Mishneh).
the damager swears a heset oath. An oath enacted by the Sages for one who is sued and denies everything (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3).
and it will all be one field. And he will be able to work both plots together.
for their holding them back in this matter is the trait of Sodom. A reprehensible trait, for no loss would come to them from it (as above 7:8).

and they valued the good against the bad. They assessed the worth of its various parts in relation to their quality, so that there is a part good in quality and small in area compared with parts poor in quality and large in area.
give me, at my valuation, from this side. He asked to receive the portion adjacent to his other field.

they do not listen to him. For each of them could prefer that either the small good portion or the large poor portion fall to his share, and there is no trait of Sodom here (R. Yosef Migash, Bava Batra 12b).

give me half its measure from the poor side without valuation. He is willing to take from the poor portion of the field adjacent to his field without their reducing the area of the field's good portion (ibid.).
some Geonim ruled that they listen to him. For both sides gain from it, and if they refuse, there is an element of the trait of Sodom.
the firstborn who divided. With his brothers the estate of their father, and he is entitled to a double portion of the inheritance (Hilchot Nachalot 2:1).
takes his two portions as one. Even if the portions are not equal (some portions being good and some poor), the firstborn takes his two portions together (Maggid Mishneh).

but the yavam who divided with his brothers the father's estate etc.. One who performs levirate marriage with the wife of his brother who died childless inherits all his brother's property, but is not entitled to take the two portions as one (Hilchot Nachalot 3:7-8).

and if they came up for him in two places, they came up. If all the portions were equal, the yavam takes his portion in one place, because we compel against the trait of Sodom (Maggid Mishneh, as explained in the previous halakhah).
a square piece of land that had etc.. An area surrounded by a river on two sides and roads on two sides, where each of the sharers wants to receive a portion of the river and the road.
and if he said etc.. After they divided the area diagonally.
to one. To another person who is not one of the brothers or partners.
they remove the buyer. They may compel the buyer to give up his right to the land when he receives its value from them.
on the side of the border. Whose property borders the property that was sold.
an agent of the neighbor. To buy the land from the seller (and see below 13:7).
whether his agent sold. The landowner's agent.
or the court sold. For example, they sold it to collect a debt owed by the landowner.
and the sale is the same. The seller wishes to sell his field, and it makes no difference to whom he sells.
it is good and right that he buy this place etc.. And he will be able to work his fields easily.
if the neighbors were many. Several fields belonging to different people surround the field being sold.
it is divided among them according to their number. They divide it among themselves by the number of neighbors.
to one of his partners in business. His partner in commercial matters.
even though he is not his partner in the land, he acquired it. For it is good and right that a person do business with his partner (R. Yitzchak ibn Giyyat and other Rishonim, Bava Metzia 108b).

for he bought it and others as one. Because it is convenient for the seller to sell all his property to one person, in this case the Sages did not enact the law of the neighbor (Meiri, Bava Metzia 108b). It is possible to explain that since it is a single transaction that also includes fields that do not border the neighbor, just as he cannot remove the buyer from those fields, so he cannot remove him from the neighboring field.

one who sells to the original owners. Because returning the land to its original owners is a greater fulfillment of doing what is right and good than selling to the neighbor, for he returns the land to the one who was forced to sell it (Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Metzia 108b).
one who buys from a gentile. For certainly a Jewish neighbor is preferable to a gentile neighbor (see Babylonian Talmud, ibid.).

one who sells to a gentile. One who sells to a gentile a field adjacent to the fields of Jews; the seller himself does not thereby transgress 'doing what is right and good', since this law applies to the buyer (see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 108b).
they excommunicate him. They place him under a ban.
contrary to the law of Israel. Which goes against Jewish law, even though under gentile law he is exempt.

renting is not subject to etc.. If the field's owner wants to rent it to another, the neighbor cannot demand that the renter remove himself from the rental so that he may rent it instead. All the more so, a person who holds property as a renter cannot demand priority on the basis of being a neighbor (Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that when a person rented property to another and now wishes to sell the property to the renter himself, the neighbor cannot hold him back (Kesef Mishneh based on Maggid Mishneh).
one who takes a place as a pledge. It was given to his creditor as security, so that if he does not repay the loan, he will take it.
it is not subject to the law of the neighbor. Because the holder of the pledge has a more direct connection to the property than the neighbor.
and likewise one who sells a distant place in order to redeem a near place. He sells a field far from his residence or from his other fields in order to buy with its proceeds an adjacent field.
in order to pay the king's tax. A tax paid to the king.
for burial. For the burial needs of one of his family members.
for the sustenance of his wife or daughters. Whom he must provide with sustenance.

for all of these are pressed to sell and sell out of great need. For a further implication of this matter (regarding a sale for the king's tax, for burial needs, or for the sustenance of the wife and daughters), see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 12:11.
the neighbor must bring proof. Because the buyer is in possession of the field and the neighbor comes to take it from him.
even if there was a doubt in the matter etc.. When the buyer claims that the neighbor has no right to remove him because he is not the owner of the land.
a sharecropper. A person who received the field to work for a certain percentage of the crop.
one who sells to minor orphans, the law of the neighbor does not apply. The neighbor cannot prevent the orphans from buying.
a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered, so it is not apparent whether he is male or female.
and an androgynos. One who has both male and female organs, and the Sages did not decide whether he has the law of a male or a female (Hilchot Ishut 2:24).
and the building or the trees. That are on the same land.
a right in the land. For example, one who buys three trees (Hilchot Mechirah 24:1).
a row of date palms. A continuous row of date palms.
if he can bring in etc.. If there is vacant land connecting the fields of the width of one furrow.

the law of the neighbor does not apply to it. One who gives a gift wishes to give it specifically to the recipient and not to another person, so doing what is right and good for the neighbor does not apply in this case.
for the liability for this gift rests on the giver. That if it is taken from him, he will give him its value.

since it carries liability, it is a sale, and he wrote 'gift' only to cancel the right of the neighbor. For givers do not usually accept liability for a gift, and presumably he gave it as a gift in order to trick the neighbor.

and how much does he give him? What it is worth. When the buyer does not admit that it was a sale and therefore does not state the amount he paid, the neighbor gives the recipient of the gift its value.
he swears while holding a sacred object. While holding a Torah scroll in his hand (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).

like the law of agents. Since the buyer is like the neighbor's agent (as above 12:5), he must swear that he is not deceiving the neighbor, like an agent who swears that he did not rob his principal (see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 9:5).

but if he said, 'I bought something worth a hundred for two hundred,' he is not believed. Even with an oath, for the presumption is that a person does not buy land for double its value, and if we believed the recipient in this case, a person would sell and call it a gift, and the recipient would deceive by claiming he bought it for a large sum (Maggid Mishneh).
and I accepted liability for this gift, that if it leaves his hand I will give him two hundred. The giver accepted liability to give the recipient double its value.
the neighbor gives him two hundred etc.. For presumably the giver did not accept liability for double the amount he received for the land, and that is what the recipient paid.

the law of the neighbor does not apply to it. For people are usually particular about the use of a particular courtyard, and the seller wants specifically the courtyard he received in exchange for this one (Maggid Mishneh).

he exchanged a courtyard for an animal or other movable property etc.. Since people are not usually particular about a particular animal or particular objects, the law of the neighbor applies to such an exchange.
and he cannot say to him, 'Give me the like of what I took for it'. The buyer cannot demand that the neighbor give him an animal or movables like what he gave in exchange for this courtyard.

for this is a trick and accomplishes nothing. His demand that the neighbor pay him as he paid is an attempt to prevent the neighbor from buying the land, and since people are not particular about an animal or movables, they do not listen to him.
land beside the one in the middle. And it borders the neighbor's field.
iddit. Choice quality.
zibburit. Poor quality.
the buyer acquired. Since it differs in quality from the land he first bought, we do not assume he bought it only to trick and afterward buy the rest of the field.
and no claim at all will remain in it. There will be no more claims regarding the sale, for only when the sale is complete can the neighbor remove the buyer.
but all the produce he ate before is his. For as long as the neighbor has not come to buy the field, it belongs to the buyer and the right to eat the produce is his.
and he gives him the appropriate payment. As explained in the next paragraph.

if the buyer borrowed before the neighbor removed him. Ordinarily, if a borrower has no property with which to pay his debt, the lender may collect his debt from the borrower's land even after he sold it, because it was encumbered for collection of the debt (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 18:1).
his creditor does not seize from the hand of the neighbor. Because the neighbor is not considered as buying from the borrower, but the buyer is considered his agent.

if he improved, he takes the expense. The buyer receives the expenses he paid for improving the land, but not the full increase in the land's value resulting from the improvement (see Lechem Mishneh).
they deduct for him from the payment. The neighbor reduces the cost of the damage or of the produce eaten from the price of the land.
and the neighbor came to remove him from half of it only, that he bought from the other. For he is a neighbor only with regard to this half.

he can only either remove him from all of it or leave all of it. For leaving a person with half a field is not doing what is good and right (Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 175:9), or because it is a single transaction and its half alone cannot be cancelled.
an agent who sold and he is the neighbor. The field's owner sent his neighbor to sell the field adjacent to his own.

a creditor of the seller who seized the field from the neighbor. After the neighbor removed the buyer, a creditor of the landowner came to collect his debt from this land, which had been encumbered for the debt.

the neighbor etc.. Although the buyer is considered the neighbor's agent (above halakhah 7), he is not truly his agent, and he bears liability for the sale, and therefore the neighbor can claim from him that he pay him the value of the field that was seized from him (Or Sameach, and see Kesef Mishneh).
the neighbor may remove him. The neighbor can give the creditor the money value of the field and remove him from the field he seized.

the power of the one who seizes should not be greater than the power of the buyer. Therefore, just as the neighbor has the power to remove the buyer, so he has the power to remove the creditor who seizes the land in collecting a debt.

and if the one from whom it was seized wishes to give the money etc.. Even after the neighbor removed the creditor, if the original owner of the field wishes to pay the neighbor the money he paid the creditor, the field returns to his hands. The reason is that the neighbor's power should not be better than the power of a creditor, and just as the land returns from a creditor, so also from the neighbor.

as will be explained in its place. That owners always have the right to pay their debt and receive back the land that was collected from them, because of 'doing what is right and good' (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 22:16).
they remove the buyer for him. Because a minor does not know how to claim for himself.
or they take for him a share with the other neighbors. In a case where there are other neighbors of the land that was sold.
a husband whose wife was the neighbor. Land adjacent to the land she brought with her in marriage is up for sale.

even if they made a kinyan from his wife, who waived this right to the buyer. They made a kinyan that she waives the neighbor's right, and ordinarily such a kinyan is effective to cancel the neighbor's right (below 14:2).
it is not effective. For the wife's waiver cannot cause her husband to lose his rights in the land.
and she removed the buyer. In place of the husband, by the law of the neighbor.
if the husband or the master wished etc.. The husband or the master has the right to decide whether he wishes to uphold the transaction that his wife or his slave made (see Hilchot Mechirah 30:2-3).
and the one who wishes to buy from him. The prospective buyer.
I will go to the trouble and bring. He has no cash on hand and wants to go to the effort of collecting money.
they do not listen to him. For the neighbor has no right to hold up the sale.
I will go and bring. Money from home.
assessed as having. Estimated to be wealthy.
for no time is fixed for the neighbor. Unlike a borrower who requests time to obtain money before they seize his property (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 22:1).
better than his zuzim. Of better weight or appearance.
or ones that go out faster than his zuzim. Because of their quality they pass quickly to a merchant.
for the sake of the settlement of the land. For building houses is preferable for developing the land to agricultural sowing.
and he consulted the neighbor. He consulted with him.
they made a kinyan from his hand. They made a kinyan sudar that he cancels his right (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
and helped him. In that same land he bought.
and uses. Or uses.
in another country, or ill, or a minor. And therefore could not remove the buyer.
and on this the Geonim ruled. In this manner.
one who sells something worth two hundred for a maneh. The buyer bought land worth two hundred and paid a hundred for it, and when the neighbor claimed the land, the buyer asked two hundred for it.
if he sells cheaply to everyone. If the landowner sold it for a maneh regardless of this particular buyer, for example, he sold it because of financial pressure.
he bought something worth a hundred for two hundred. The buyer bought the land for double its value.
for this is collusion between them. The buyer and seller schemed to extract another hundred from the neighbor and split the profit between them.
the buyer swears while holding a sacred object. While holding a Torah scroll in his hand (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
that it was an agreement. They agreed between themselves.
and he has him swear a heset oath that he bought for two hundred. The neighbor has the buyer swear, for a heset oath is administered on a claim of certainty (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:7).
and he is released. The buyer does not have to return to the neighbor the hundred he claims from him.
and none of them is a neighbor. And the neighbor does not wish to buy.
from the residents of the city. From the townspeople.
from the dwellers of the field. From those who live in the field.
the city neighbor takes precedence. Because they are people of the same city and closer to one another.

a neighbor and a relative - the neighbor takes precedence. As it says, 'A near neighbor is better than a distant brother' (Proverbs 27:10, Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 108b; for a similar law see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 11:3).
for the Sages did not command in this matter as a matter of law. As they established the law of the neighbor.
